newsitem.title: USA: Motorola EPS beats estimates, revs off.
newsitem.headline: Motorola EPS beats estimates, revs off.

text.p: Motorola Inc pleasantly surprised the market with better-than-expected earnings and a jump in the gross margin, but analysts said revenues were shy of expectations.

"The bottom line is these are pretty good numbers," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst for Gruntal & Co. "The margins are improving, they're bringing costs down and it's an improving trend. But revenue is the question mark right now."
Earlier, Motorola posted first quarter earnings of $325 million or $0.53 a share versus $384 million or $0.63.
Revenues were $6.6 billion compared with nearly $7.0 billion last year, and analysts said they were expecting from about $6.8 billion to $7.2 billion.
Motorola said the $0.53 a share included gains on the sale of an investment and a favorable patent settlement, but those gains accounted for less than 10 percent of pre-tax profits.
Excluding the gains, Motorola earned at least $0.48 a share, analysts estimated.
According to First Call, the consensus of analysts' estimates was $0.45 a share.
"They beat estimates," said Douglas Christopher, an analyst with Crowell, Weedon & Co. "It looks like management is doing an extremely good job of managing in this difficult time."
Analysts said they were impressed with an unexpected jump in the gross margin to about 34 percent from just over 32 percent.
"I think the bottom line was they were able to reduce their costs," said Chris Chaney, an analyst for A.G. Edwards. "Gross margin was up a couple of points and we didn't expect that."
Analysts pointed to lower sales in semiconductors, paging and space and systems technology as the reason for the lower than expected revenues.

Motorola said Semiconductor Products Segment sales were down 16 percent versus last year, Messaging Information and Media Segment, which includes the paging group, posted a decline of seven percent, and the Space and Systems Technology Group sales fell 43 percent.

Also, analysts said they will look for guidance in a conference call with the company early on Tuesday as to the effect of the stronger dollar, which may have also pressured revenues. Some 58 percent of Motorola's total sales were from outside the United States in 1996.
"It's a mixed bag," said Robert Wilkes, an analyst for Brown Brothers Harriman. "Revenues were less than expected but earnings were a little more."
Although semiconductor profits were below last year, Motorola said the segment returned to profitability in the first quarter after posting an operating loss in the fourth quarter of 1996.
"You're seeing gradual signs of improvement in sequential profitablity (in semiconductors)," Christopher said. "They're saying it has emerged from the recession."
Overall, analysts said they had looked for sequential improvement over the fourth quarter of 1996, which they saw. In the fourth quarter Motorola reported earnings of $0.39 a share.
